message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This brief draws on six months of trial data from three independent sources, the operator's ticketing system, its vehicle-location data and our own traffic counters, compared against a matched pre-trial period, with the settling-in month excluded so that early disruption does not flatter or penalise the scheme. The results are consistent and strong: morning bus journeys 22% faster, punctuality up from 71% to 84%, and an 18% rise in weekday boardings that brings in roughly £302,000 a year of extra fare revenue, which the operator has committed to reinvest. Just as important for members, the counters show that general traffic was essentially unaffected, which answers the main political objection to bus lanes before it is raised. We have also dealt carefully with the traders' delivery concerns through two new loading bays. The consultation shows majority support, and the equalities case is clear given low car ownership on the corridor. I am confident this is a well-evidenced, low-cost decision that Committee can take with assurance.
</author>

<document>
Policy Brief: Making the Elm Road Bus Lane Permanent
City Transport Department, for the Transport and Environment Committee, May 2026

Recommendation
That the Committee approve a permanent traffic order for the Elm Road bus lane, replacing the experimental order that expires on 31 August 2026, and approve £85,000 for permanent signage, road markings, loading bays and an enforcement camera.

Background
Route 14 is the city's busiest bus route, linking the Northgate estates with the city centre along Elm Road. Before the trial, buses on the corridor were routinely delayed in queues on the 2.4 km section between the ring road and Market Square, and Route 14 had the worst punctuality of any route in the network.

In September 2025 the Department introduced an experimental bus lane on both the city-bound and outbound sides of that section, in force from 7 to 10 am and from 4 to 7 pm on weekdays. Outside those hours the lane is available to all traffic and for parking and loading. Data from the operator's ticketing and vehicle-location systems and from the Department's automatic traffic counters were compared for March to July 2025 and October 2025 to March 2026; September was excluded as a settling-in month.

Table 1. Route 14 and Elm Road corridor, average weekday
Measure | Before (Mar-Jul 2025) | Trial (Oct 2025-Mar 2026)
AM peak bus journey time, city-bound (min) | 24.5 | 19.0
PM peak bus journey time, outbound (min) | 26.0 | 22.5
Weekday boardings, Route 14 | 6,200 | 6,950
Buses departing on time | 71% | 84%
AM peak general traffic journey time, city-bound (min) | 18.0 | 19.5
Recorded injury collisions (per six months) | 7 | 6

Findings
Bus journey times fell substantially in both peaks. The city-bound morning journey is now 5.5 minutes quicker, a reduction of 22%, and the outbound evening journey is 3.5 minutes quicker, a reduction of 13%. Punctuality improved from 71% to 84% of departures on time, moving Route 14 from the worst-performing route in the network to above the network average of 80%.

Passengers have responded. Average weekday boardings rose by 750, an increase of 18%. Over a year of 252 weekdays this is 189,000 additional trips; at the average fare yield of £1.60 per boarding, the additional fare revenue to the operator is around £302,000 a year, which the operator has agreed to reinvest in a 10-minute evening frequency on Route 14 from January 2027.

Importantly, the scheme has achieved this without penalising other road users. General traffic journey times on the corridor were essentially unchanged over the trial, as drivers adapted their routes and timings. Recorded injury collisions fell slightly, from seven to six over equivalent six-month periods; the numbers are too small to draw firm conclusions on safety, but there is no sign of deterioration.

Consultation
A statutory consultation ran from 2 February to 16 March 2026 and received 412 responses: 241 supporting permanence (58%), 139 opposing (34%) and 32 neither (8%). Support was strongest among bus users and residents of the Northgate estates. The main concern among objectors was access for deliveries to the 23 shops on the Elm Road parade. Loading on the lane is permitted outside its operating hours of 7 to 9 am and 4 to 6 pm, and the Department has met the traders' association to agree two additional loading bays in adjacent side streets, which are included in the £85,000.

Costs and enforcement
The permanent scheme requires replacement of temporary signs and markings (£41,000), the two loading bays (£12,000) and a fixed enforcement camera (£32,000), a total of £85,000, to be met from the Local Transport Plan capital allocation. Penalty-charge income during the trial covered the cost of manual enforcement, and the camera is expected to reduce the need for officer patrols.

Equalities
Route 14 serves the two most deprived wards in the city, where 46% of households do not have access to a car. Faster and more reliable buses on this corridor therefore benefit residents who have the fewest alternatives.

Conclusion
The trial has delivered faster and more reliable buses and a substantial increase in patronage, at no measurable cost to general traffic and with majority support in consultation. Making the lane permanent is a low-cost, high-value step consistent with the Local Transport Plan's objective of growing bus use on the city's radial corridors. We recommend that the Committee approve the permanent order and the associated £85,000 capital spend.
</document>
response:
The brief asks Committee to make the Elm Road bus lane permanent, at a cost of £85,000. It cites faster and more punctual buses, an 18% rise in boardings worth about £302,000 a year, no effect on general traffic, and majority support in the consultation.

The bus improvements are large and well supported, and the case for approval probably holds. But two of the headline claims misread the brief's own Table 1. Boardings rose 12%, not 18%. General traffic journey times rose 8%, which is not "essentially unchanged." The lane's operating hours are also stated two different ways, and the difference matters for the traders. And the before and after periods cover different seasons, so they aren't a matched comparison.

## 1. What checks out

- **Morning bus journey:** 24.5 → 19.0 minutes is 5.5 minutes quicker, a 22% reduction.
- **Evening bus journey:** 26.0 → 22.5 minutes is 3.5 minutes quicker, a 13% reduction.
- **Revenue arithmetic:** 750 extra boardings × 252 weekdays = 189,000 trips. At £1.60 a boarding, that is about £302,000.
- **Consultation:** 241 + 139 + 32 = 412 responses, which is 58% support, 34% opposed and 8% neither.
- **Costs:** £41,000 + £12,000 + £32,000 = £85,000.
- **Collisions:** the brief is rightly cautious about the change from 7 to 6.

## 2. Boardings rose 12%, not 18%

6,200 → 6,950 is a rise of **750, or 12.1%**. An 18% rise would mean about 1,116 more boardings a day.

The £302,000 figure is calculated from the 750, so it is unaffected. The 18% appears in the Findings and in the author's description.

A 12% rise in under a year is still a strong result, so correcting it costs the case nothing.

## 3. General traffic was not "essentially unchanged"

Table 1 shows morning general-traffic journeys city-bound rising from **18.0 to 19.5 minutes, an 8% increase**. That is a modest cost, and it may be a price worth paying. But the brief says traffic was "essentially unchanged," and the author's description calls it "essentially unaffected." Both say the opposite of what the table shows.

**The brief also leaves out two traffic measures:**
- **Evening outbound general traffic.** No figure is given, even though the lane runs on both sides of the road.
- **Side streets.** The brief says drivers "adapted their routes and timings." That suggests traffic may have moved onto nearby streets, which the corridor counters wouldn't pick up.

Councillors who object to bus lanes will find the 19.5 in the table. It's better for the brief to present the 1.5 minutes honestly and set it against 5.5 minutes saved on every bus.

## 4. The lane's hours are stated two ways

- **Background:** in force **7–10 am and 4–7 pm**.
- **Consultation section:** "outside its operating hours of **7 to 9 am and 4 to 6 pm**."

The difference is two hours a day of loading access, which is the traders' main concern. Confirm the correct hours. If 7–9 and 4–6 were given to the traders' association, correct that with them before the decision.

## 5. The before and after periods aren't matched

The brief compares **March–July 2025** with **October 2025–March 2026**. These are different times of year:

- Winter traffic is usually heavier and slower. That could make the bus gains *understated*, and it could explain some or all of the 1.5-minute rise in general traffic.
- Bus use varies by season and weather, so part of the boardings change may be seasonal.
- Network-wide trends, such as fare changes or growth in bus use generally, aren't controlled for.

**Stronger comparisons:**
- October 2024–March 2025 against October 2025–March 2026, the same months a year apart;
- or Route 14's change set against network-wide or comparable routes over the same period;
- or, for punctuality, whether the network average was 80% before the trial too.

The bus improvements are large enough that they will very likely survive this check. The traffic and boardings figures are less certain.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Revenue goes to the operator, not the council.** The £302,000 doesn't offset the £85,000. The operator's commitment to reinvest it in a 10-minute evening frequency is the real benefit to residents, and it's worth confirming that commitment in writing.
- **"Three independent sources."** The data is drawn from all three sources as described. But it was compared across different seasons, so "matched" overstates it.

## How the author's description compares

| Author's claim | Holds? |
|---|---|
| Three sources, compared against a matched pre-trial period | The sources yes; "matched" no, because the periods cover different seasons |
| Morning journeys 22% faster, punctuality 71% → 84% | Yes |
| 18% rise in boardings | No. 12% (750 on 6,200) |
| About £302,000 extra fare revenue | Yes, from the 750 figure, though some of the rise may be seasonal |
| General traffic essentially unaffected | No. Morning journeys up 1.5 minutes (8%); evening traffic and side streets not reported |
| Traders' concerns dealt with through two loading bays | Bays agreed, but the brief gives conflicting lane hours |
| Majority support in consultation | Yes, 58%. Responses come from people who chose to take part |
| Clear equalities case | Yes |
| Well-evidenced, low-cost decision | Low-cost yes. The evidence needs the corrections above |

## Recommendation

**Approval looks justified on the corrected evidence.** The bus gains are large: 5.5 minutes off the morning journey and a 13-point rise in punctuality. They benefit residents with the fewest alternatives, and the traffic cost is modest. Before the brief goes to Committee:

1. **Correct the boardings rise** to 12%.
2. **Replace "essentially unchanged"** with the actual 1.5-minute (8%) rise, and add evening traffic and side-street data if available.
3. **Settle the operating hours**, and confirm them with the traders' association.
4. **Add a same-season or comparison-route check**, or acknowledge the seasonal limitation.
